list.listitem: Order liver function tests, hepatitis serology, a CBC with platelets, and a prothrombin time (PT) test if a liver abnormality is suspected. Additional testing may include alpha-1-antitrypsin studies, transferrin saturation and total iron binding capacity (TIBC), ANA, and ANCA. C

Abdominal ultrasound shear-wave elastography is the first-line imaging study for diagnosing cirrhosis; magnetic resonance elastography abdomen or diagnostic liver biopsy can be considered if ultrasound is inconclusive. C
Patients with chronic liver disease should abstain completely from alcohol. B
Propranolol (40-80 mg twice daily) is recommended for prophylaxis of variceal bleeding. B

Treatment of complications includes sodium restriction, A diuretics, A and possible transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) or surgical shunt for ascites; B lactulose syrup, flumazenil, and possibly neomycin or rifaximin for hepatic encephalopathy (HE); and antibiotics for patients with 250 PMNs or greater in their ascitic fluid and for those who survive an episode of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP). A
An early referral to a transplant subspecialist is recommended. C

background.definition: Cirrhosis refers to a progressive, diffuse, fibrosing, nodular condition that disrupts the normal architecture of the liver. Fibrosis refers to the scarring process formed in response to inflammation or direct toxic insult to the liver.

list.listitem: In a study of 508 patients with HIV and chronic hepatitis B or C, cirrhosis occurred in 10.6% over 2 to 3 years; risk of cirrhosis was low in patients who cleared HCV with therapy or those on long-term HBV suppressive therapy.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), about 1.8% or 4.5 million U.S. adults are diagnosed with liver disease (2018).
A total of 17,206 persons with cirrhosis are awaiting a liver transplant in the United States.
Cirrhosis and chronic liver failure were the 11th most common cause of death in the United States in 2017 and the 10th leading cause of death in men. (CDC)
Accounted for 41,743 deaths or 12.8 per 100,000 (CDC, 2017).
Among 145 patients undergoing endoscopy for cirrhosis, a split-sample prospective study found that 45% had esophageal varices.

Acute kidney injury (AKI) occurs in about 29% of patients with cirrhosis and is associated with an increased risk of both in-hospital mortality (OR 5.90; 95% CI 3.21-10.85) and mortality up to 1-year after development of AKI.

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) occurred in 10% of trial participants with liver cirrhosis, 15% of whom died, based on a Cochrane review of 29 RCTs evaluating prophylactic antibiotics for prevention of SBP. In addition, approximately 2.5% of hospitalizations in people with liver cirrhosis are for SBP.

While ischemic stroke is uncommon, at 3.7% in patients with cirrhosis, authors of a meta-analysis found a higher risk of subarachnoid (HR 2.36; 95% CI 1.80-3.09) and intracranial hemorrhage (HR 1.48; 95% CI 1.06-2.05) in these patients.

Both chronic liver disease and chronic kidney disease increase severity of COVID-19 disease. Authors of a meta-analysis of 22 studies with 5595 patients with COVID-19 found severe disease in 57.3% (43/75) of patients with underlying liver disease and 17.6% died compared to an overall case fatality rate of 16%.
Alcohol: 60% to 70%.
Hepatitis B or C: 10%.
Biliary tract disease (biliary cirrhosis, biliary atresia, cystic fibrosis, congenital biliary cysts): 5% to 10%.
Hemochromatosis: 5% to 10%.
Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD): 10%.

Rare causes: autoimmune chronic hepatitis, drugs and toxins, genetic metabolic disease (eg, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, bile acid disorders, Wilson’s disease), granulomatous liver disease, idiopathic portal fibrosis, infection (brucellosis, schistosomiasis, echinococcosis, syphilis), and vascular problems (right-sided heart failure, hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, and venoocclusive disease).
Single or multifactorial insults to the liver ultimately lead to cirrhosis; alcohol abuse, chronic hepatitis (B or C), and obesity with concomitant NAFLD are the most common etiologies.

Genetic susceptibility: Based on a prospective UK cohort study including 414,209 subjects, there was a synergistic interaction for those who were homozygous for a genetic variant I148M in the patatin-like phospholipase domain-containing protein 3 gene plus had obesity and excessive alcohol intake increasing the risk of cirrhosis compared to those with none of these three, with an adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 17.5; 95% CI 12.8-23.9. Similar increased risk was observed in this population for hepatocellular carcinoma and liver disease-related mortality.

The common pathway to cirrhosis is diffuse destruction of hepatic parenchyma and its replacement with collagenous scar tissue and regenerating nodules, leading to disruption of the normal hepatic lobular and vascular architecture.
Regardless of the specific etiology of cirrhosis, the triad of parenchymal necrosis, regeneration, and scarring is present in all patients.
Eliminate alcohol consumption to prevent progression in patients with chronic liver disease; 75% to 80% of cirrhosis cases could be prevented by eliminating alcohol abuse. B
Use universal precautions and immunization (hepatitis A and B) to minimize contraction of viral hepatitis in patients with cirrhosis. B

Authors of a meta-analysis found that antibiotic prophylaxis with a quinolone against nosocomial bacterial infections (eg, UTIs, peritonitis, pneumonia, primary bacteremia) reduces risk of death (NNT = 19) in hospitalized patients with end-stage liver disease. A See Drug Therapy section below.

Patients with cirrhosis and GI hemorrhage, cirrhosis and ascites, or acute on chronic liver failure should receive prophylactic antibiotics (norfloxacin or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole twice daily for 7 days) to prevent bacterial infections (including SBP) and possibly reduce the number of deaths.B Data are less clear about the benefit of antibiotics for prevention of SBP in other patients with cirrhosis.

A meta-analysis of fourteen RCTs involving patients with cirrhosis who present with acute upper GI bleeding found that a shorter duration (2 to 3 days) of antibiotic prophylaxis, including no prophylaxis at all, is noninferior to a longer duration (5 to 7 days) for mortality prevention, but may lead to a higher incidence of early rebleeds and bacterial infections.

Based on data from a National Cancer Registry and National Death Registry Database in Taiwan, initiation of nationwide neonatal hepatitis B vaccinations (since 1984) and national antiviral therapy programs for patients with hepatitis B and C (since 2003) were associated with reductions in chronic liver disease mortality (adjusted rate ratio [aRR], 0.7; 95% CI 0.7-0.8), hepatocellular carcinoma incidence (aRR 0.47; 95% CI 0.4-0.5) and hepatocellular carcinoma mortality (aRR 0.5; 95% CI 0.45-0.0.45-0.6), with a sharply declining association by cohort comparing the 1982 to 1986 birth cohort to the 2007 to 2011 birth cohort.

In a large retrospective cohort study, patients with alcohol-use disorder, use of any medical treatment (i.e., disulfiram, acamprosate, naltrexone, gabapentin, topiramate, or baclofen) reduced the development of alcoholic-associated liver disease and hepatic decompensation for those with alcoholic-associated liver disease (adjusted OR [aOR] 0.37; 95% CI 0.31-0.43 and aOR 0.35; 95% CI 0.23-0.53, respectively). Patients in the treated group were significantly more likely to be female (4444% vs. 36%), white (85% vs.83%), have a history of homelessness (15.4% vs.6.5%), viral hepatitis (16% vs.9.9%), receipt of psychotherapy (50.6% vs.30.4%), and non-alcohol substance-use disorder (49.8% vs. 27.6%).

A VA study matched patients with and without cirrhosis who were taking a GLP-1 receptor agonist with an equal number of patients taking a dipeptidyl peptidase 4 inhibitor (DPP-4i). Patients without cirrhosis taking a GLP-1 were significantly less likely to develop cirrhosis (10 vs 11 events/1000 person-years). For those who already had cirrhosis there was no association between GLP-1 use and outcomes.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 29 RCTs with 3896 participants using nine antibiotic regimens to prevent SBP in patients with cirrhosis concluded that antibiotics did not influence mortality, SBP or number of serious adverse events (very low certainty). There was some evidence that rifamixin or norfloxacin plus neomycin use resulted in fewer other decompensation events (low certainty).

Authors of a Bayesian network meta-analysis of 17 RCTs of prophylactic antibiotics in patients with cirrhosis and ascites found benefit for primary prevention of SBP using norfloxacin daily (OR 0.06; 95% CI 0.006-0.33), rifaximin daily (OR 0.037; 95% CI 0.00085-0.87) and norfloxacin and rifaximin in alternate months (OR 0.027; 95% CI 0.0006-0.61) compared to placebo or no comparator, and for rifaximin for secondary prevention (OR 0.022; 95% CI 0.00011-0.73).

Patients with cirrhosis and GI hemorrhage who received prophylactic antibiotics (norfloxacin or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole twice daily for 7 days) to prevent bacterial infections (including SBP) had fewer infections and possibly fewer eaths.

Similar to the Taiwan study above, patients with chronic hepatitis C treated with direct-acting antiviral-treatment compared to untreated patients had a decreased incidence of liver outcomes per 1000 patient-years including decompensation 28.2 (95% CI 27.0-29.4) vs 40.8 (95% CI, 40.1-41.5) and hepatocellular carcinoma in those with compensated cirrhosis 20.1 (95% CI 18.4-21.9) vs 41.8 (95% CI 40.3-43.3). All-cause mortality rates per 1000 person-years were also significantly lower in treated patients (36.5, 95% CI 35.4-37.7 vs 64.7, 95% CI 63.9-65.4). Treated patients were more likely to have baseline cirrhosis (17, 971/40,654 [44%] vs 60,094/204,942 [29%]).
A randomized trial with 143 patients who had acute on chronic liver failure found that norfloxacin reduced the risk of bacterial infection.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 12 studies with 43,532 patients with alcoholic liver disease or cirrhosis found that use of direct oral anticoagulants (DOAs) compared to warfarin or low molecular weight heparin was associated with reduced rates of recurrence/progression of deep vein thrombosis (pooled hazard ratio [HR] 0.18; 95% CI 0.06-0.57) but no differences in stroke or all-cause death. DOAC reduced incidence of major bleeding (HR 0.39; 95% CI 0.21-0.70) including intracranial hemorrhage (HR 0.48; 95% CI 0.40-0.59), but not any bleeding or GI bleeding.

An observational propensity score matched analysis of US claims databases identified patients with cirrhosis and non-valvular atrial fibrillation who were starting a direct oral anticoagulant. Major hemorrhage was significantly more common in persons starting rivaroxaban than apixaban with a risk difference of 33 more events per 1000-person-years (HR 1.47, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.94). There was no difference in rates of ischemic events or death.

Order liver function tests, a CBC with platelets, and a PT test if a liver abnormality is suspected. Additional testing may include alpha-1-antitrypsin studies, transferrin saturation, TIBC, ANA, and ANCA. C

If serum transaminase levels are greater than twice the upper limit of normal or remain elevated for longer than 6 months (or if clinical suspicion for liver disease is high), order additional serologic studies. C
Abdominal ultrasound shear-wave elastography is recommended as the first-line radiographic study for diagnosing cirrhosis. C
If clinical, laboratory, and radiographic data are inconclusive but suspicion of cirrhosis remains, then a diagnostic liver biopsy should be performed. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Abrupt onset of malaise, fever, anorexia, jaundice, abdominal pain, dark-colored urine, and light-colored stools
Severely impaired liver function with encephalopathy and coma in patients with liver disease <8 weeks; high morbidity and mortality; liver transplant may be considered

list.listitem: See for the Child-Turcotte-Pugh (CTP) scoring system to assess liver disease severity.
A 2012 systematic review provides positive and negative predictive values, sensitivity and specificity of various clinical indicators of cirrhosis in patients with liver disease.
Early and well-compensated cirrhosis can manifest as anorexia and weight loss, weakness, fatigue, and osteoporosis resulting from vitamin D malabsorption and subsequent calcium deficiency.
Decompensated disease results in ascites, SBP, HE, and variceal bleeding from portal hypertension.
Clinical symptoms at presentation may include jaundice of the eyes or skin, pruritus, edema, gastrointestinal bleeding, coagulopathy, increased abdominal girth, and mental status changes.

If ascites is suspected, signs and symptoms that best rule it in when present are fluid wave, shifting dullness, or telangiectasias. Absence of bulging flanks, edema, or increased girth best rule it out.
Subacute hepatic necrosis is suggested by ascites, edema, or hepatic coma.

Initial laboratory evaluation should include liver function tests, a CBC with platelets, PT, hepatitis serology, ferritin, serum iron, TIBC, and albumin. Suspect alcoholic liver disease based on history, AST/ALT ratio >2, and elevated gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT).

If initial tests are nondiagnostic and the patient is symptomatic, consider ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody (ASMA) to rule out autoimmune hepatitis, serum alpha-1-antitrypsin and/or genetic screening, and serum ceruloplasmin and serum copper. Patients with Wilson's disease have low serum ceruloplasmin (<20 mg/dL) or low serum copper (<80 mcg/dL). Measure basal 24-hour urinary copper excretion (normal 10-80 mcg, over 100 mcg in patients with Wilson’s disease), and consider genetic screening.

Severe fibrosis or cirrhosis in patients with hepatitis C are suggested by AST/ALT ratio ≥1, platelet count <140,000/mm3, or both.A platelet count <160,000/mm3 is 80% sensitive for detecting cirrhosis. For patients with chronic hepatitis B, the best predictor of liver cirrhosis was the red cell distribution width-to-lymphocyte ratio with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.87. In another study of patients with chronic hepatitis B, the total bile acid-to-cholesterol ratio at a cut-off value of 2.7 was a good predictor of cirrhosis with an AUC of 0.87.

Among patients with hepatitis D genotype III, the fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) calculator using a cut-off value of 1.36, determined based on the patient’s age, AST, ALT and platelet count, and the AST to platelet ratio index (APRI) using a cut-off value of 0.708 were useful for predicting liver fibrosis.

NAFLD is an uncommon cause of cirrhosis and usually occurs in patients with the progressive form - nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH); suspect in patients with diabetes who are morbidly obese. Usually requires biopsy to confirm diagnosis.

Authors of a recent review of non-invasive diagnostic options found that none of the biomarkers had sufficient sensitivity or specificity for differentiating NASH from NAFLD, although combination approaches are promising. Of the imaging options, magnetic resonance elastography is most promising; these tests appear most useful for ruling out advanced fibrosis.

In a VA hospital cohort, the FIB-4 was the best non-invasive scoring system for predicting biopsy-proven NAFLD with advanced fibrosis with an AUC using a 2.67 threshold of 0.62 to 0.80 and positive likelihood ratio of 4.7 to 27.5.
Among 118 patients with primary biliary cholangitis, the total bile acid to platelet ratio appeared useful for predicting liver fibrosis, with an AUC of 0.77.
Esophageal varices are suggested by the ratio of platelet count (platelets/mm3) to maximum spleen diameter in millimeters, measured by ultrasound; 71% of patients with a ratio ≤909 had varicies.

Elevated alpha-fetoprotein suggests hepatocellular cancer (HCC). A new serum marker, Golgi protein 73 (GP73), appears to be accurate for the detection of HCC and its recurrence after surgery; sensitivity (74.6% vs 58.2%) and specificity (97.4% vs 85.3%) were higher than for AFP. Although GP73 levels were elevated in HBV carriers and patients with cirrhosis, they were much lower than in patients with HCC.
Clinically significant portal hypertension is more likely in patients with liver stiffness measurement >= 25 kPa, except in patients with HBV.

Imaging is used to detect complications of cirrhosis, including ascites, hepatosplenomegaly, hepatic or portal vein thromboses, and hepatocellular carcinoma, all of which strongly suggest cirrhosis. Ultrasound transient elastography ("FibroScan") for liver stiffness measurement (LSM) can be used to exclude bridging fibrosis and cirrhosis. The American College of Radiology (2019) recommends ultrasound shear-wave elastography abdomen or magnetic resonance elastography abdomen for patients with chronic liver disease for diagnosis and staging of liver fibrosis.

In one study, LSM was more accurate than the aminotransferase-to-platelet ratio index for cirrhosis (AUC 0.88) with a sensitivity and specificity for cirrhosis (prevalence 11%) of 96% and 81%, respectively (using a cut-off of 11.1 kPa).
FibroScan was also the best predictor of liver fibrosis in a study of 116 patients with concomitant chronic hepatitis B and NAFLD with an AUC of 0.87.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 8 studies found the newer XL probe to be more reliable than the m probe for ultrasound transient elastography (TE) with a sensitivity of 0.56 (95% CI 0.39-0.72), specificity of 0.71 (95% CI 0.61-0.79), and an AUC of 0.71 for liver fibrosis stage ≥F2 and a sensitivity of 0.84 (95% CI 0.76-0.90), specificity of 0.78 (95% CI 0.70-0.84), and an AUC of 0.88 for liver fibrosis stage F4.

In the most recent meta-analysis of 29 diagnostic studies in patients with non-viral hepatopathies, elastography using acoustic radiation force impulse (ARFI) had a pooled sensitivity of 0.79; 95% CI 0.73-0.83 and specificity of 0.81; 95% CI 0.75-0.86, with an AUC of 0.87; 95% CI 0.83-0.89 for staging of significant fibrosis. These values were even higher when staging for cirrhosis (0.89, 0.89 and 0.94, respectively).

In a study of 62 adults with biopsy-proven NAFLD, shear-wave elastography, TE and MR elastography had comparable and very good to excellent diagnostic accuracy for advanced fibrosis with AUCs of 0.89 (95% CI 0.80-0.98), 0.86 (0.77-0.95), and 0.95 (0.89-1.00), respectively. AUCs for significant fibrosis were of comparable but lower accuracy.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) had an area under the ROC curve of 0.90 for the diagnosis of fibrosis, with a correlation coefficient of 0.75. Sensitivity and specificity were approximately 85%.

Gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI for the staging liver fibrosis was evaluated in a meta-analysis of 20 papers and had AUCs for liver fibrosis ≥F1, ≥F2, ≥F3, and F4 subsets of 0.92, 0.87, 0.89, and 0.91, respectively.
Diagnostic abdominal paracentesis should be performed and ascitic fluid obtained from patients with clinically evident ascites.

Two systematic reviews, one with 8 studies and 116,000 patients and one with 7 studies and 78,000 patients, both found that early diagnostic paracentesis was associated with lower in-hospital mortality (aOR 0.61 to 0.69), shorter length of stay (4.8 to 5.4 days shorter) and improvements in other secondary outcomes.

Liver biopsy is used in patients with suspected cirrhosis for whom non-invasive testing is inconclusive. The American Association for the Study of Liver Disease (AASLD) 2019 guideline on alcohol-associated liver disease recommends biopsy in patients with possible alcoholic hepatitis and confounding factors such as uncertain alcohol use history, atypical laboratory tests, or possible drug-induced liver disease or ischemic hepatitis. The AASLD 2019 guidelines on adults with autoimmune hepatitis recommend histologic confirmation for these patients and recommend evaluation for advanced fibrosis using non-invasive markers or liver biopsy, if required, for all patients with HCV infection to facilitate treatment decisions.
The CTP scoring system is shown in and is used to assess the severity of liver disease.
The MELD score can be used for prognosis in patients with end-stage liver disease and as a guide to decision-making regarding transplant.
A second clinical rule has been developed and validated to predict the presence of cirrhosis in patients with chronic hepatitis C infection.
See chapters on hepatitis C and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease for additional clinical decision rules related to chronic liver disease.
The CLIF-C ACLF score can be used to determine prognosis.

Non-invasive scoring systems are less useful for evaluating NAFLD-associated fibrosis among individuals in the general population. In a database study in Sweden, the 10-year incidence of developing cirrhosis or its complications was 1% to 1.4% and was increased in intermediate- and high-risk groups with hazard ratios in the high-risk group ranging from 1.67 for the BARD score (AST/ALT ratio, BMI, and presence of diabetes) to 45.9 for the APRI score. Scores were more predictive in patients with NAFLD risk factors.
The FibroScan-AST (FAST) score was 89% sensitive and 89% specific for predicing fibrotic NASH in patients with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
The aMAP risk score can predict the risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma in patients with chronic liver disease.

A risk score with age, sex and 6 laboratory variables can identify persons in the general population at increased risk for liver-related mortality, hospitalization, and hepatocellular carcinoma. It was prospectively validated and had an AUC of 0.83.
Suspect cirrhosis in patients with signs and symptoms of chronic liver disease (eg, anorexia, fatigue), persistent abnormalities on liver function testing, or incidental abnormal imaging studies.

Initial laboratory evaluation should be performed (see Diagnostic testing). If the initial laboratory tests are normal and patient is asymptomatic, the patient can be treated with 6 months of life-style intervention.
If the patient is symptomatic or laboratory abnormalities persist, proceed to ultrasound as the initial imaging test.
If the diagnosis is uncertain, consider liver biopsy.
Emphasize complete abstention from alcohol. A
Give propranolol (40-80 mg twice daily) for prophylaxis of variceal bleeding. B

Give antibiotics (eg, cefotaxime 2 g IV q 8 h) for patients with ascitic fluid PMN counts ≥250 cells/mm3; patients with cirrhosis who survive an episode of SBP should receive long-term antibiotic prophylaxis with norfloxacin or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. A
Refer early to a transplant subspecialist. C

Propranolol at a dose of 40 mg twice daily is recommended for pharmacologic prophylaxis of variceal bleeding, increasing to 80 mg twice daily if necessary or a dose titrated to a 25% reduction in pulse rate.

However, authors of a systematic review of 3 RCTs and 13 observational studies found no difference in survival, likelihood of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, or hepatorenal syndrome incidence with the use of nonselective beta-blockers.
Although antibiotics are usually recommended, there is no clear evidence to guide their selection or treatment duration in patients with cirrhosis and SBP.

Patients with cirrhosis who survive an episode of SBP should receive long-term antibiotic prophylaxis with norfloxacin (400 mg once daily) or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (one single-strength tablet daily).
Using a systematic review of 9 observational studies and 1 RCT, authors concluded that statins may retard progression of fibrosis and hepatic decompensation (HR ~0.5).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 11 primarily case-control studies and 6 RCTs found statin treatment improved survival rate (HR 0.782; 95% CI 0.718-0.846) and reduced cirrhosis complications including risk of hepatic encephalopathy, ascites and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC, HR for 0.75; 95% CI 0.64-0.86); statins had no influence on risk of esophageal variceal bleeding or SBP. There was no increase in drug-related adverse events observed.

While dose-dependent effects of statins were seen on HCC development, occurrence of decompensated cirrhosis, and liver cirrhosis progression in the above study, these results should be interpreted with caution as there was moderate to considerable heterogeneity between studies, demonstrated by I2 values >50%. The single long-term RCT included, however, found no difference in the primary endpoint of a composite of bleeding or death, but did find increased survival with statins. In this trial, 17 patients (22%) in the placebo group died vs 6 (9%) patients in the simvastatin group (hazard ratio 0.39; 95% CI 0.15-0.99).

A complication of rhabdomyolysis occurred in 3 of 18 subjects in a phase-2 trial of combination simvastatin 40 mg/day plus rifaximin compared to the 20 mg dose or placebo in patients with decompensated cirrhosis. The investigators suggest using the lower dose in future trials.
Authors of a Cochrane review of 13 RCTs found that flumazenil had a significant beneficial effect on short-term improvement of HE in patients with cirrhosis but had no effect on recovery or survival.
Propylthiouracil and colchicine do not improve outcomes in patients with alcoholic liver disease.

A phase 2b trial randomized 181 participants with compensated cirrhosis (stage 4 fibrosis) to efruxifermin (a fibroblast growth factor) or placebo. The drug did not significantly reduce fibrosis at 36 weeks (18% vs 13%).

A single small RCT (n=100) randomized patients with hepatic decompensation to allopurinol 300 mg or placebo once daily for 6 months. The likelihood of overt ascites (HR 0.33, 95% CI 0.01-0.76) and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (HR 0.25, 95% CI 0.05-0.76). Given the unexpectedly large effect this requires replication.

A phase-1 trial of a single infusion of autologous macrophage therapy to potentially reduce liver fibrosis was completed in 9 adults with cirrhosis and a MELD score of 10-16. No immediate complications occurred and, at one-year, all patients are alive and transplant-free with only one clinical event recorded, the occurrence of minimal ascites.
Ursodeoxycholic acid is first-line treatment for patients with primary biliary cirrhosis, with obeticholic acid as second-line therapy.

TIPS should be considered in patients with refractory ascites who may require liver transplant. Authors of a meta-analysis found that TIPS (vs paracentesis) was more effective at removing ascites, but there was no difference in mortality, GI bleeding, infection, or acute renal failure. Also, more patients developed HE.

Surgical shunting (eg, portocaval shunt) is another option. Authors of a systematic review of three prospective RCTs and one retrospective case-controlled study of patients with CTP classes A or B found better 2-year survival (OR = 2.5; 95% CI 1.2-5.2) and less frequent shunt failure (OR = 0.3; 95% CI 0.1-0.9) in patients undergoing surgical shunting compared with TIPS.

In an RCT, early use of TIPS (within 72 hours of diagnosis) in patients with advanced cirrhosis and acute variceal bleeding, reduced mortality at one year (1-year survival rate: 86% in the early TIPS group vs 61% in the standard treatment group; NNT = 4; 95% CI 2.1-50). Early surgery also prevented rebleeding or failure to control bleeding (1 patient vs 14 patients at 16 month follow-up) without increasing the frequency or severity of HE. Another RCT demonstrated that covered stents versus uncovered improved shunt patency and overall survival.

In an RCT of 49 patients with cirrhosis, primarily CTP class A or B, portal vein thrombosis and an episode of variceal bleeding, those randomized to TIPS compared to endoscopic band ligation plus propranolol had significantly less rebleeding at 2 years (25% vs 50%) but no significant difference in overt HE (25% vs 16%) or survival (67% vs 84%).

A second RCT identified 100 patients with Child-Pugh class B or C cirrhosis who presented with acute variceal bleeding. There was no difference in survival between 8-mm covered TIPS versus endoscopic variceal ligation plus propranolol groups. Variceal rebleeds were less likely with TIPS (HR 0.31, 95% CI 0.14-0.69), but overt hepatic encephalopathy was more likely with TIPS (30.0% vs 16.0%, p = .03).
Consider a peritoneovenous shunt in patients with refractory ascites who are not candidates for paracenteses, transplant, or TIPS.

In a nonblinded RCT, endoscopic ligation proved more effective than propranolol at preventing variceal bleeding; however, rates of death and hospitalization were not significantly affected and the procedure is highly intensive and expensive.

Available evidence supports the use of glycyrrhizin (licorice root extract) in the treatment of subacute liver failure and in the prevention of hepatocellular carcinoma in patients with chronic active hepatitis C.

In a 3-month pilot RCT of 70 patients with liver cirrhosis of whom 60 completed the study, curcumin supplementation, an herb found in turmeric, decreased disease activity and severity scores (MELD and Child-Pugh) in patients with cirrhosis compared to placebo.
There is insufficient evidence to support the use of milk thistle for patients with alcoholic and/or hepatitis B or C virus-associated liver disease.
There is insufficient evidence to support or refute the use of S-adenosyl-l-methionine for patients with alcoholic liver disease.
Authors of a Cochrane review of 17 trials found no benefit of emergency sclerotherapy for variceal bleeding in patients with cirrhosis compared with vasoactive drugs.
Exercise interventions 3 to 5 times weekly may improve walking distance without adverse effects.
No benefit on quality of life or hospitalization days was found for self-management programs based on a systematic review of 4 low-quality RCTs.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis found zinc supplementation of benefit for clinical improvement of HE based on three studies. There was no mortality benefit from zinc supplementation in another review of four studies.

Longer duration treatment with norfloxacin was evaluated in an RCT of 291 patients with Child--Turcotte-Pugh class C cirrhosis (Table 1) who had not received recent fluoroquinolone therapy. Treatment had no significant effect on 6-month mortality (14.8% vs 19.7%, respectively) but appeared to increase survival among patients with low ascites-fluid protein concentrations.
Patients should be referred early to a transplant subspecialist to allow time for the patient, family, referring physician, and transplant center to meet and identify any potential problems.
Transplant care is best provided by a team of healthcare professionals including a hepatologist, a surgeon, a psychiatrist, and a social worker.

The initial assessment of a possible transplant recipient should incorporate education highlighting the risks and benefits of organ transplantation, including the potential for poor outcomes (eg, organ rejection) and standard posttransplant care and follow-up.
Predictors of transfer to the ICU included worsening renal function, anemia, hyponatremia, leukocytosis, and having obtained a lactate level.
Common complications addressed in more detail in other chapters include ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, esophageal varices, and hepatorenal syndrome.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 12 RCTs with 1278 participants found no differences between antibiotics - primarily third-generation cephalosporins such as intravenous ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, or ciprofloxacin - on mortality, proportion of people with any adverse events, resolution of SBP, or other features of decompensation (very low certainty). About 75% of patients recovered and 25% died within 3 months. Authors of a systematic review call for attention to infection site, organisms such as fungi, and emerging bacterial resistance as further considerations in choice of antibiotic in patients with cirrhosis.

First-line treatment of patients with cirrhotic ascites consists of sodium restriction (eg, maximum of 2000 mg/day) and diuretics (oral spironolactone with or without furosemide) as well as complete abstention from alcohol. Fluid restriction is not necessary unless serum sodium is <120 to 125 mmol/L.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 49 RCTs with 3521 participants found only low-quality evidence to support use of diuretics or TIPS. Just over one third of patients in the control group using paracentesis plus fluid replacement died within 11 months and no treatment demonstrated a benefit in mortality, adverse events, or liver transplantation. Greater resolution of ascites was demonstrated adding aldosterone antagonists to paracentesis plus fluid replacement (HR 30.63; 95% credible interval [CrI] 5.06-692.98) or for TIPS (HR 9.44; 95% CrI 1.93-62.68). Combination aldosterone antagonist plus loop diuretic had a higher rate of other decompensation events (eg, HE, hepatorenal syndrome) and variceal bleeding compared to controls.

In one study of hospitalized patients with cirrhosis, intravenous high-dose furosemide (250-1000 mg twice daily) plus small-volume hypertonic saline solution (150 mL 1.4%-4.6%) resulted in better diuresis and weight loss than repeated paracentesis for refractory ascites; the long-term effectiveness and mortality benefit of this treatment is unknown.

In an Italian randomized, open label trial of 431 hospitalized patients with persistent ascites due to hepatic cirrhosis, those who received human albumin infusions in addition to standard medical therapy had longer overall survival at 18 months (83% vs 78%, respectively; NNT = 24) and improved quality of life than those treated with standard medical therapy of spironolactone and furosemide alone.

Authors of a systematic review of 30 low-quality RCTs found that use of terlipressin significantly improved control of bleeding within 48 hours (OR = 2.94) and decreased in-hospital mortality (OR = 0.31).
Adding variceal embolization to TIPS did not significantly reduce the incidence of variceal rebleeding in an RCT including 134 patients with cirrhosis.

The 2026 American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) guideline on hepatic encephalopathy recommends treating patients with HE with lactulose to improve patient outcomes and prevent recurrence (strong recommendation, moderate certainty), or with high volume polyethylene glycol as an alternative to lactulose (conditional recommendation, low certainty). The guideline also suggests adding oral rifamixin to lactulose therapy (conditional recommendation, low certainty).

HE is treated with 30 to 45 mL of lactulose syrup orally titrated up to 3 to 4 times/day or 300 mL retention enema until the patient has 2 to 4 bowel movements/day and mental status improves. Polyethylene glycol 3350-electrolyte solution (PEG) appears to be a safe and effective alternative to lactulose. Neomycin (4-12 g orally per day divided every 6-8 hours) can be added if the encephalopathy is refractory to lactulose alone.

However, authors of a systematic review and network meta-analysis of 25 trials with 1563 patients with cirrhosis found moderate-quality evidence for reversing minimal HE compared with placebo or no treatment for rifaximin (OR 7.53; 95% predictive interval [PrI] 4.45-12.73) and lactulose (OR 5.39; 95% PrI 3.60-8.0). Low-quality evidence supported use of combination probiotics and lactulose (OR 4.66; 95% PrI 1.90-11.39), L-ornithine L-aspartate (OR 4.45; 95% PrI 2.67-7.42), and probiotics (OR 3.89; 95% PrI 2.52-6.02). Agents effective in preventing episodes of overt HE compared with placebo or no treatment included L-ornithine L-aspartate (OR 0.19; 95% PrI 0.04-0.91; high to moderate quality), lactulose (OR 0.22; 95% PrI 0.09-0.52; moderate quality), and probiotics (OR 0.27; 95% PrI 0.11-0.62; low quality).

In an RCT of patients with recurrent HE and a model for end-stage liver disease (MELD) score of 25 or less, rifaximin (550 mg twice daily, in addition to lactulose) reduced breakthrough episodes of HE (22.1% rifaximin group vs 45.9% placebo group); four patients would need to be treated with rifaximin for 6 months to prevent 1 episode of HE (NNT = 4; 95% CI 3-6). Risk of HE in patients with chronic liver disease is increased with use of proton pump inhibitors (OR 2.31; 95% CI 1.63-3.28) based on one meta-analysis.
Portal hypertension (hepatic venous pressure gradient ≥10 mm Hg)
Portal hypertension can be managed with propranolol 40 to 80 mg daily and isosorbide mononitrate 20 mg orally twice daily.

In an RCT of 201 Spanish patients with compensated portal hypertension without high-risk varices, those randomized to a beta-blocker (67 to propranolol and 33 to carvedilol due to non-response to propranolol) had a significantly lower rate of decompensation or death than those on placebo (16% vs 27% respectively) at a median follow-up of 37 months; this difference was primarily due to a lower rate of ascites (9% vs 20%, respectively).

This syndrome is characterized by acute hepatic decompensation, often triggered by infection, alcohol use, or recurrent hepatitis. Mortality is high, especially with increasing organ system involvement and failure. Patients should be admitted to ICU and preferably managed in a transplant center, and assessed for transplant.
The CLIF-C ACLF score can be used to determine prognosis.
Granulocyte colony stimulating factor therapy and stem cell therapy have been explored in small trials and are considered experimental.
There is no demonstrated benefit to administration of albumin to patients with extraperitoneal infection with respect to mortality or renal function based on a meta-analysis of 3 RCTs.

A randomized trial identified 777 patients hospitalized with decompensated cirrhosis. Patients were randomized to infusions of 140 to 280 g albumin in the high dose group versus 20 to 120 g in the standard care group. There was no difference between groups.

A study identified 143 patients with acute on chronic liver failure and randomized them to norfloxacin 400 mg once daily or placebo for 30 days. At 30 days, there was a lower risk of bacterial infection (18% vs 34%, p = 0.03, NNT = 7) and also at 90 days (46% vs 62%, = .02, NNT = 7).

In a systematic review including eight studies with 353 patients comparing anticoagulation with placebo or no treatment in patients with portal vein thrombosis, authors found a higher rate of partial and complete canalization with anticoagulation. Studies, however, were at high risk of bias due to lack of randomization and masking.

Loss of muscle mass or sarcopenia occurs with aging as well as chronic diseases including liver cirrhosis. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of seven studies including Asian participants and 13 studies including Western participants with cirrhosis found a prevalence rate of sarcopenia of 48.1%; prevalence rate was higher in men than women (61.6% and 36%, respectively). Sarcopenia was associated with increased complication rates and poorer survival with a mortality HR for Asians of 2.45; 95% CI 1.44-4.16 and HR Westerners of 1.45; 95% CI 1.002-2.09.

Limited evidence supports use of leucine or leucine-enriched proteins (range 1.2-6 g leucine/day) co-administered with vitamin D for improving sarcopenia in elderly individuals; however, the effect on muscular strength is mixed and the effect on physical performance is unknown.

A systematic review of 12 RCTs found that cramp frequency is decreased to some extent by a variety of treatments, including the muscle relaxants baclofen, methocarbamol, and orphenadrine; the amino acid taurine; branched-chain amino acids; human albumin; pregabalin; quinidine; and calcium carbonate. Pickle juice (1–3 tablespoons daily) decreases cramp severity. Stretching, meditation, and electroacupuncture have little to no effect.

Patients with ascitic fluid PMN counts ≥250 cells/mm3 should receive empiric antibiotic therapy (eg, cefotaxime 2 g intravenously every 8 hours) and albumin (1.5 g per kg body weight within 6 hours of detection and 1 g per kg on day 3) to prevent SBP.

Authors of a meta-analysis found that antibiotic prophylaxis with a quinolone against nosocomial bacterial infections (eg, UTIs, peritonitis, pneumonia, primary bacteremia) reduced risk of death (NNT = 19) in hospitalized patients with end-stage liver disease.

In an Italian randomized, open label trial of 431 hospitalized patients with persistent ascites due to hepatic cirrhosis, those who received human albumin infusions in addition to standard medical therapy had longer overall survival at 18 months (83% vs 78%, respectively; NNT = 24) and improved quality of life than those treated with standard medical therapy of spironolactone and furosemide alone.
Patients who consume excessive alcohol or are older than 38 years are more likely to progress to end-stage disease. B

A prospective cohort study found that patients who consume excessive alcohol or are older than 38 years are more likely to progress to end-stage liver disease.
Fibrosis may be reversible to a degree in some patients with hepatitis B after treatment with antiretroviral therapy.

The CTP scoring classification (), originally devised to risk-stratify patients undergoing TIPS surgery for portal decompression, is useful to assess severity of liver disease in patients with cirrhosis.

In a retrospective study involving 92 patients with cirrhosis who underwent abdominal surgery, the mortality rate was 10% for patients with CTP grade A disease, 30% for those with grade B disease, and 82% for those with grade C disease.

Overall mortality for treated hepatitis C patients in the contemporary era of interferon-free treatment regimens remain about 3 times higher than the general population, a study that looked at patients in Canada, Scotland and England concluded. The main drivers of this increased mortality were drug and liver-related causes of death including hepatocellular carcinoma. Being older, having recent substance or alcohol misuse, and comorbidities were associated with higher mortality.

Risk factors for development of hepatocellular carcinoma in patients with cirrhosis were determined based on a multivariate analysis of 1723 patients with cirrhosis who were followed for a median 2.2 years (range 0 to 9 years). Risk factors included male gender (OR 2.5), more years with cirrhosis, family history of liver cancer (OR 2.7), increasing age (OR 1.17 per 5 years), obesity (OR 1.7), elevated AST, elevated alpha-fetoprotein, and decreased albumin.

The statistical model for end-stage liver disease (MELD) predicts survival in patients with cirrhosis and has been adopted for routine use in the timing and allocation of transplantation. Patients with a MELD score of 40 out of 50 points have a 3-month survival rate of less than 20%.

A prediction model including respiratory failure, renal failure, international normalized ratio, total bilirubin, and neutrophil count was successful in predicting 90-day mortality in patients with advanced cirrhosis and concomitant infection in both a US and Korean cohort with an AUROC of 0.808 and 0.809, respectively. Mortality rates ranged from 54% to 58%.

Investigators using a retrospective study of 1438 critically-ill patients with cirrhosis and suspected infection found the highest accuracy for predicting in-hospital mortality using chronic liver failure/Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (CLIF-SOFA; area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROCC] 0.74), CLIF-consortium organ failure (AUROCC 0.74), or Simplified Acute Physiology Score II (AUROCC 0.76).

Elevated plasma von-Willebrand factor (vWF), an endothelial activation marker, was evaluated as a prognostic marker in patients with chronic liver disease. Based on 6 studies with 765 patients, baseline plasma vWF-antigen was an independent predictor of 1 to 3-year mortality in patients with cirrhosis (AUC 0.74; 95% CI 0.70-0.79) with an optimal cut-off of 318% over a period of 25.6 months.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 studies with 4428 patients with biopsy-proven NAFLD, of whom 2875 were reported to have NASH, found unadjusted risk increased with increasing stage of fibrosis (stage 0 vs 4) for all-cause mortality (RR 3.42; 95% CI 2.63-4.46), liver transplant (RR 5.42; 95% CI 1.05-27.89), and liver-related events (RR 12.78; 95% Cl 6.85-23.85) compared to patients with NAFLD and no fibrosis.

In a 4-year follow-up study of 430 patients with chronic hepatitis B, 29 (6.7%) developed liver-related complications of cirrhosis. Liver stiffness measured with 2-D shear-wave elastography as a single measure had the highest AUC of 0.86; 95% CI 0.82-0.89; this AUC was not significantly different than the multivariable model using elastography, spleen longitudinal diameter at ultrasound, age, and albumin level.

Loss of muscle mass is also associated with increased mortality in patients with cirrhosis; in a meta-analysis of 16 observational studies with 4070 participants, OR was 1.68 (95% CI 0.96-2.92) in those with CTP class B and 1.94 (95% CI 0.66-5.65) in those with CPT class C.
Use of proton pump inhibitors is associated with increased long-term mortality (but not short-term) in observational studies.

Obtain an alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and ultrasound every 6 months to monitor for HCC in patients with CTP class A or B cirrhosis and chronic liver failure.In a prospective study of 392 patients with cirrhosis who underwent routine AFP and US screening, 64 (16.3%) developed HCC at a mean age of 53.6 years. Use of both tests was associated with the highest sensitivity of 89.1% with high specificity of 94.5%.

In a case-control study of 476 patients with cirrhosis, however, there were no significant differences between the 238 cases who died of HCC and 238 matched controls in the proportions of patients who underwent screening ultrasound (52.9% vs 54.2%), screening serum AFP (74.8% vs 73.5%), both screening tests (46.6% vs 48.3%) or either (81.1% vs 79.4%).

Authors of a paper reviewing these findings noted high rates of comorbidities in patients attending VA hospitals, making most poor candidates for radical treatment, and pointed to observational studies demonstrating earlier-stage tumors identified through surveillance. One such retrospective study of 680 patients with cirrhosis, of whom 78 (11.5%) developed HCC during the 3-year study period, found higher proportions of early HCC (70.2% vs 40%) among surveillance-detected patients. Of note, however, were high rates of physical harm (27.5% of patients) for false-positive or indeterminate surveillance tests that were more often related to ultrasound than AFP.

Ultrasound findings predictive of HCC transformation from a cirrhotic nodule in one study included initial size and delayed arrival time of contrast of >0.5 seconds between the liver and the nodule on initial contrast-enhanced ultrasound.
Alternatives to ultrasound also deemed appropriate by ACR for screening and surveillance for HCC are MRI abdomen without and with IV contrast or MRI abdomen without and with hepatobiliary contrast.
Patients with CTP class C are unlikely to benefit from surveillance.

feature.caption: Child-Turcotte-Pugh Scoring System to Assess Liver Disease Severity.
feature.feature_body:
Clinical and Laboratory Measurements Points Scored for Increased Abnormality
1 2 3
Encephalopathy (grade) None 1-2 3-4
Ascites None Mild (or controlled by diuretics) At least moderate despite diuretic treatment
Prothrombin time (seconds prolonged) <4 4-6 >6
OR
INR <1.7 1.7-2.3 >2.3
Albumin (g/dL) >3.5 2.8-3.5 <2.8
Bilirubin (mg/dL) <2 2-3 >3
Interpretation: A score of 5-6 = grade A; 7-9 = grade B; 10-15 = grade C. INR = International Normalized Ratio. Adapted from Davern TJ, Scharschmidt BF. Biochemical liver tests. Feldman M, Friedman LS, Sleisenger MH, eds. Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, Management, 7th ed. Philadelphia, PA: Saunders; 2002: 1236.
